question: Does this change improve our service, here, and how should we adapt it?

taylor2013.cite: Taylor et al. (2013). Systematic review of the application of the plan–do–study–act method to improve quality in healthcare. BMJ Quality & Safety 23(4): 290–298.
taylor2013.checked: every quote read word for word in the open-access full text from Europe PMC (PMC3963536, full-text XML) on 20 Nov 2026; places are the article's sections and tables; reference citations are left out.; year, volume, issue and pages as the XML gives them

steps.title: Plan
steps.text: Choose one change, say what you predict it will do, and plan who tests it, where and when.

quotes.text: A prediction of the outcome of a change is developed in the ‘plan’ stage of a cycle.

steps.title: Do, small
steps.text: Try the change on a small scale first: one clinic, one shift, a few patients. Note what goes wrong.

quotes.text: As certainty of success of a test of change is not guaranteed, PDSAs start small in scale and build in scale as confidence grows.

steps.title: Study over time
steps.text: Plot the measure at regular intervals before and after the change, on a run chart, and compare it with the prediction.

quotes.text: measurement of data over time helps understand natural variation in a system, increase awareness of other factors influencing processes or outcomes, and understand the impact of an intervention.
quotes.where: section “The origins and theory of PDSA cycles”

quotes.text: Methods for understanding variation within the data, including the effects of time as a variable.

steps.title: Act
steps.text: Adopt the change, adapt it, or drop it, and use what you learned to plan the next cycle.

quotes.text: the ‘act’ stage identifies adaptations and next steps to inform a new cycle.
quotes.where: section “The origins and theory of PDSA cycles”

steps.title: Cycle again
steps.text: Link the cycles: each one builds on the last, at a larger scale as confidence grows.

quotes.text: two or more cycles with lessons learned from one cycle linking and informing a subsequent cycle
quotes.where: section “Iterative cycles”, its definition of a sequence of iterative cycles

history-trend.text: Approach used to establish whether the observed outcomes were due to the intervention(s).

limits: Taylor et al. review how PDSA was applied, not how it should be done; the steps follow the method's key features as their framework (table 2) sets them out.
Run-chart rules for telling a real shift from noise are not given: no source for them was read for this page.
